discovery: Atomic-resolution non-contact atomic force microscopy with the qPlus sensor, enabling imaging of the chemical structure and bonds of single molecules
subfield: Condensed matter physics / scanning probe instrumentation
motivation: Giessibl achieved true atomic resolution by frequency-modulation AFM on Si(111)-7x7 and invented the qPlus sensor, a stiff quartz tuning-fork force transducer allowing stable oscillation at sub-angstrom amplitudes, where short-range chemical forces dominate. Building on this, Gross, Meyer and co-workers (Science 2009) functionalised the tip with a single CO molecule and resolved the complete chemical structure of a pentacene molecule, imaging individual covalent bonds in real space for the first time. Subsequent work by these groups measured bond orders, charge states of single atoms, and followed on-surface chemical reactions step by step. This is a measurement invention of the highest order: a quantitative force sensor, interpreted through careful models of tip-sample interaction, that turned a long-held textbook abstraction, the chemical bond, into a directly observable object. The qPlus technique is now a standard instrument in laboratories worldwide, across physics, chemistry and materials science.
